symptoms: Brown spots can develop on tomato leaves.
Spots may show concentric ring patterns.
Disease can cause affected leaves to yellow and die.
management: Remove and destroy severely affected plant material.
Maintain good field sanitation.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness where possible.

symptoms: Small brown spots can develop on tomato leaves.
Leaf spots may have yellow halos.
Severe disease can cause affected leaves to drop.
Water-soaked spots can develop on green fruits.
management: Use disease-free seed.
Maintain good field sanitation.
Remove and destroy severely affected plant material.

symptoms: Dark, water-soaked lesions can develop on tomato leaves.
Lesions can enlarge rapidly under favorable conditions.
Affected leaves can become brown and die.
Dark lesions can also develop on tomato fruits.
management: Remove and destroy severely affected plant material.
Maintain good field sanitation.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness where possible.

symptoms: Pale yellow-green spots can develop on the upper surface of tomato leaves.
Olive-green to brown velvety growth can develop on the lower leaf surface.
Affected leaves can wither and die.
In severe cases, blossoms and fruit can also be affected.
management: Improve air movement around plants.
Avoid watering foliage where possible.
Reduce excessive humidity around plants.
Remove crop residue at the end of the season.

symptoms: Small circular brown spots can develop on tomato leaves.
Spots can have light gray or tan centers with dark margins.
Small dark specks can develop in the centers of leaf spots.
Severely affected leaves can drop prematurely.
management: Remove affected leaves and plant debris.
Improve air circulation around plants.
Keep foliage as dry as possible.
Avoid overhead watering where possible.

symptoms: Small white to yellow stippling or speckling can develop on tomato leaves.
Affected leaves can become brown and dry as feeding continues.
Leaves may curl as damage becomes severe.
Webbing can develop on the undersides of leaves when mite populations are high.
management: Inspect new plants regularly before introducing them into the growing area.
Inspect the undersides of leaves for mites and webbing.
Encourage natural enemies such as lady beetles, lacewings, and predatory thrips.
Use water to help dislodge mites from affected plants where appropriate.
